extra.reason: Resolved by composting rather than by choosing. A bd memory is the highest-intent record bd produces - one sentence someone decided should outlive its session, written for no other purpose - so the pile mines it from transcripts alongside commit messages and bead closes. It composts as a discovery at lower confidence than a recorded change, because a memory is an assertion with no diff behind it and may be written by an agent. bd keeps memories for priming; the pile keeps them for every other project.

The bridge reads work from bd and never writes it: bd owns beads, dependencies and the ready queue, hugel owns knowledge and accounting. Beds are located from transcript cwd rather than configuration, since a bed is already named for a working directory. Readiness comes from bd directly rather than being recomputed, so hugel's view cannot drift from the queue tenders pull from. Surfaced through hugel bed list, which now shows where each bed lives and what is ready, active and blocked there.

One screen across every bed: in flight, ready, blocked, with tab switching to the knowledge side. Built as panes on the tend model rather than a second TUI, because work and knowledge are two halves of one sitting. Read-only - bd owns starting and closing a bead. Per-bed caps keep one busy bed from burying the others, and each pane keeps its own cursor position.

A tender is an ordinary interactive agent session running detached in tmux, briefed by a file and answering with a file - not claude -p, and no send-keys. That keeps it on a subscription and leaves both the request and the outcome on disk for review. Each tender gets a worktree and branch of its own, named for the bed rather than the bead so transcript accounting stays with the project. It commits to its branch and stops: pushing, merging and closing are the gate's decisions.

A tender's brief now carries soil drawn for the bead, with the caveat that it is a survey rather than the truth. Push is right here and pull is right in interactive sessions for the same reason: where the tokens land and who is there to ask. The bead's full text scores the draw; its title labels it, because the rendered header quotes the query back into the brief.

Deleted. They describe the Postgres, DBOS and Firecracker system this rewrite exists to escape, and were never committed, so git history carries neither. What survived the plan is already in the pile as composted decisions: the ordering argument, the durable-execution reasoning, and the reason all of it was too much canopy for the roots that existed.

Work, test, review, test, then merge, push and close. The second test runs on the branch merged with the current base, which is the only test true of what gets pushed. The reviewer is a separate agent run with a different prompt and is forbidden from repairing what it finds, since doing both leaves nobody to review the repair. A review with no verdict counts as refusal - silence is not approval. Every stage refuses without cleaning up, so a failed gate leaves the work where it can be read.

Measured: bd prime --hook-json emits 6506 bytes, about 1626 tokens, injected at turn zero of every session. Carried across the 12 sessions of the last week (1461 turns) that is 2.4M context tokens, ~$1.19 of $289.29 spent, or 0.4%. Per session it ranges 0.3-0.7%. The preamble is worth it: an agent that does not know about ready work cannot pick any up, and 0.4% is not the waste worth hunting - the 86% context tax is. This also sets a yardstick for hugel's own soil budget, which at 1500 tokens is the same order of magnitude and should be held to the same test. Caveat: this prices the carrying only. Whether the preamble changes how many turns a session takes is a different and harder question, unmeasured here.

A skill that drafts beads and epics in conversation, reviews them with the user, and files only what is agreed. Filing unreviewed work fills the queue with intentions, which matters more now that tenders pull from it unattended. Most of the skill is about what makes a bead worth filing: the description carries the why rather than restating the title, because closing a bead with a reason is what the pile composts, so a bead is paid for twice.

A dispatcher rather than a daemon: it counts working tenders, starts more from the ready queue until the slots are full, and exits, so anything that can repeat can drive it and nothing has to survive a crash. Priority wins across beds so a long backlog cannot starve the others, ordering is stable so two dispatches cannot race for different beads, and an exclusive file create stops them running at once. Dispatch also reaps tenders that died holding a bead - the failure nothing else in the system notices - releasing the bead while keeping the worktree as evidence.

Measured before building, and bd carries most of the load. This session produced 2 compostable records on 24 Aug and produces 22 now; the only change is that work is tracked in bd and beads are closed with reasons. The extractor's total catch went from 142 entries to 162 on the strength of one session's bead closes. Seven sessions still compost to zero and all seven are in one bed, tourdesource - sessions that neither committed nor closed a bead with a reason. That residue is not extractor blindness but an absence of deliberate records, and no amount of model-backed extraction invents a record nobody wrote. A model extractor is therefore not justified yet: the cheap fix is closing beads with reasons, which is free, already happening, and produces higher-precision entries than prose ever would.

All seven children landed: the bd bridge, the garden screen, the tender, soil in its brief, the gate, and the dispatcher. The loop runs end to end - draft a bead, dispatch a tender into a tmux worktree with soil in its brief, gate the work through test-review-test, merge and push, close the bead, and compost the reason into the pile that briefs the next tender. What made it small enough to finish was refusing the parts the v2 design said were required: no daemon, no database, no durable execution layer. A dispatcher that exits, a lock file, and files at both ends of every agent.

The acceptance criteria bd has been recording all along now reach both briefs. The reviewer answers them one at a time before anything else, and an unmet criterion blocks a pass regardless of what else is good - which turns 'is this good work', a judgement an agent answers agreeably, into a question with an answer. They are presented as a floor rather than a ceiling so a reviewer does not stop reading the code once the boxes are ticked, and a bead with no criteria says so rather than leaving the reviewer to invent a standard. Read fresh from bd at gate time, since a gate reviewing against stale criteria is reviewing a spec nobody holds. The tender is shown the same criteria: otherwise the two agents disagree about a standard only one was told.

A tender reporting blocked has found something about the bead rather than failed. The reason now appends to the bead in the tender's own words, the bead is released and labelled needs-attention, and dispatch leaves it alone while the mark stands - though bd ready still shows it, because it is genuinely ready for a person. A label rather than a status for exactly that reason. Release, mark and reason go in one bd call so they cannot half-happen. A second attempt archives the first rather than being refused, or 'while that mark stands' would mean forever.

yield --changes attributes tender and reviewer sessions to the bead whose worktree they ran in, and averages only over beads that landed - dividing by abandoned work would make giving up look like efficiency. Attempts count per run, so a bead handed back and tended again shows as costing twice. Two things stated where they are read rather than in a doc: the figures are equivalent API rates and not a bill, since a subscription charges for no token here, and the share of spend the report can speak for is printed beside it, because only tended work is attributable and interactive work is most of the window.

Work waiting on a person now leads each bed and the header totals, because it is the only count in the garden nothing else will act on - a tender picks up ready work unattended and never picks up a bead handed back. Attention outranks every other state rather than sitting beside them: a handed-back bead is still open and bd still calls it ready, so counting it as ready would report work as available that no tender will start. The reason it stopped is shown before its description, since for that one row the reason is what you came to read.

One wide event per unit of work, flat, in ~/.hugel/events.jsonl. Counts are derived from events and never replace them - the draw log already proved why, storing entry ids rather than a count is the only reason draw precision exists. No SDK and no spans: causality here does not cross machines, so the bead is the trace id. Emit returns nothing on purpose, since every emitter sits inside work that matters more than its own instrumentation. Inert until the gate and tenders emit, which is the order the epic argues for.

One event per gate stage carrying the detail the refusal rests on rather than a summary of it, plus gate.test tagged branch or merged, gate.review with the verdict and the reviewer's session, gate.land with the sha, and one gate.run row so a refusal is findable without walking the stages. Tested by the acceptance directly: a refusal reconstructable from events alone, and no review or land event when the gate stops earlier.

tender.start records everything known at the moment work begins -- branch, worktree, tmux session, soil token estimate, brief size, whether the bead had criteria -- and stop and handback record how the life ended, so between them every exit a tender has is on the log. Attribution to a bead becomes a record rather than an inference from directory names, which is what cost per accepted change should switch to.

hugel gate --grade reports what fraction of gate-approved landings survived, over a window. Young landings are excluded rather than counted as survivors -- a change that landed an hour ago has not survived anything. The gate now records the base sha alongside the landed one, so base..sha is exactly what a landing introduced and a branch reverted by its middle commit no longer reads as work that held. Reverts that cannot be attributed are reported outside the rate rather than dropped. A reopened bead counts against the gate as its own fate. Reporting only: nothing here makes the reviewer stricter.

yield.Attempts reads runs out of the event log and the cli keeps tender state only as a fallback for runs from before the log existed, matched by bead and start time so the same run is not counted twice. Landing is now gate.land rather than a closed bead: a bead can be closed for any number of reasons and only the gate says the change was tested, reviewed and merged -- bd is still asked about beads the gate never landed, because work merged by hand is accepted change too. A window keyed on attempt times was written and then removed: worktree paths are per-bead, so nothing reuses one and the machinery had no observable effect.

One wide event per unit of work, flat, in ~/.hugel/events.jsonl, with the bead as the trace id and no SDK. Gate stages, gate runs, tests, reviews, landings and the whole tender lifecycle are on it, and a refusal is reconstructable from events alone. Both readers the acceptance named now exist and read from it rather than from state: cost per accepted change takes runs from tender.start and landing from gate.land, and gate survival takes landings from gate.land and grades them against git. draws.jsonl was left alone, as the epic argued -- migrating live instrumentation to prove a point is a bad trade. The risk the epic named for itself, a log nobody reads, was live for exactly two commits.

A revert now writes the contradicts edge to the decision it took back, joined on the title git quotes into the revert's own subject -- entries record no commit sha, so the title is the join the pile can actually make. Nothing is linked unless the target is in the pile: a dangling edge reads as evidence until someone follows it, and a revert of work never composted is ordinary. Soil multiplies a contradicted entry by 0.2, heavier than superseded and heavier than any amount of age, because age was standing in for evidence and this is the evidence. Down-weighted rather than dropped: that a thing was tried and taken back is what stops the next tender trying it again.

beads.DiscoveredFrom reads bd's discovered-from relation upward, and gate --grade reports what was filed because of each landing beside its fate. Reported, never counted against the rate: plenty of work that held perfectly well turned something up on the way, and counting a follow-up as a failure would grade thoroughness as harm. A landing that held but turned something up sorts above one with nothing to say. The relation is written by whoever files the follow-up, which is what makes it worth reading -- a person saying this exists because of that, rather than hugel inferring a connection from two beads touching the same files.

All three the acceptance names are reported and none of them act. Cost per accepted change reads runs and landings from the event log; gate survival grades approved work against reverts, reopened beads and a maturity threshold, and reports what was filed because of each landing; a revert writes the contradicts edge to the decision it took back and soil sinks a contradicted entry below any amount of age. The epic's own caveat holds and is worth restating: these are the loud failures. A feature that works and nobody uses, or a decision subtly wrong for a year, is still invisible, and nothing here should be read as the pile knowing what worked -- it knows what visibly broke.

Guarded Running() against an empty session name so no empty target reaches tmux, and fixed the test that found it to stop the tender Start actually returned. Verified: go test -count=1 ./internal/tender/ now runs from inside tmux without killing the session.

A spike is hugel spike <bead>: the tender machinery -- worktree, detached session, a brief in and a result out -- carrying a brief that asks for knowledge instead of a diff. It records each finding with bd remember as it goes rather than at an end it may never reach, writes no code, commits nothing, closes nothing. The worktree is thrown away and what survives is what it recorded; compost already lifts bd remember into the pile as discoveries, so nothing new was needed to get a spike's knowledge home.

--attach lands on tender too. It changes one line of either brief and it is the line that matters most: whether a question is diligence or a way of parking forever. Unattended is the default for both, because that is what an agent in a detached pane actually is.

The gate refuses a spike at a new first stage, kind, before it reads the result file or looks for a test command -- so nothing downstream ever measures a spike against a tender's yardstick. The reason names what a spike is: it explores, records findings with bd remember, and leaves no diff to test, review or land.

Refused is kept apart from failed everywhere it is read. gate.run carries outcome 'refused', and the CLI says the bead is not work the gate can judge. That was the point of the bead: a spike that did its job perfectly must not be reported as work that failed.

An entry composted from a spike carries the spike's bead in its source, and hugel pile list --spike <bead> lists what one spike found (--spike any, what every spike has). The join is the worktree: it is the only thing that still connects a transcript to the bead it was exploring by the time anyone composts, and there is a test pinning it in both directions -- a spike's worktree answers with its bead, an ordinary tender's answers empty.

That last direction matters as much as the first. An entry falsely marked as a finding would be read as weaker evidence than it is, and one that lost its spike would be read as stronger.

hugel yield --spikes reports, per spike: entries produced, how many were ever drawn, how many draws, how many a person kept or threw out, and a verdict in the vocabulary the epic argued in -- never drawn, drawn and thrown out, drawn and kept.

The instrument was already there. This points yield's existing reading of the draws log and the pile at one spike's own entries, which is what the bead said would settle the question. Deliberately unflattering: an unreviewed entry counts for neither side, so a spike cannot be shown to have paid by nobody looking at it.

A spike runs over a bead as hugel spike <bead>, unattended or --attach, in the same worktree-and-tmux machinery as a tender but briefed to bring back knowledge instead of a diff. Its findings reach the pile as discoveries through bd remember, which already composted; each entry now names the spike that found it; the gate refuses to judge a spike rather than failing it for landing nothing; and hugel yield --spikes settles whether the bet paid -- never drawn, drawn and thrown out, or drawn and kept.

The clause about blocking the beads it feeds was declined rather than missed: a spike is a bead, so bd's own dependency edges already do it. See the note.

hugel tender --list now shows what a working tender has been doing: turns taken, distinct files changed, failing tool calls, and the last thing it did with how long ago. All of it read from the transcript the harness already writes -- a tender that had to report its own progress would be a tender that could lie about it.

Smoke-tested end to end against a live session, which is how two bugs in the one-line rendering surfaced.

Every review now answers a standing observability criterion alongside the bead's own, whether or not the bead states any: work that adds or changes behaviour emits one wide structured event where the work finishes, carrying the identifiers, the outcome in a word and the duration. The tender is shown the same convention before it starts, so the two agents are held to a standard both were told.

It names its own exceptions. Tests, documentation and refactors that change no behaviour answer 'met, nothing to instrument' -- a pass that makes no claim about the code. That is the difference between a criterion that gets enforced and one that gets switched off for crying wolf.

Six findings recorded, all evidence from the real pile rather than argument.

Which edge types earn their keep: contradicts, and on this evidence only contradicts. It is the one edge with both a writer that needs no human and a reader that changes behaviour. evolved_from and relates_to have neither, and relates_to duplicates what similarity ranking already does by word overlap.

Who writes them: something that already happens. The human-driven writer is measurably dead -- all 289 entries unreviewed, so supersede has never fired once. LLM inference at extraction time was already built in March, into a graph, and left nothing behind.

What would read them: a weight, not a traversal. Soil has never followed a link and does not need to; it reads contradicts into a set and multiplies by 0.2, which composes with the ranking instead of competing with it.

The worked example is the pile recording its own failed attempt: two entries dated 2026-03-24 describe adding supersedes/contradicts edge inference via a LinkRelated Cypher query, and those entries survive today as legacy-import markdown with no links, because the importer never carried any. Whatever that graph held did not outlive it.

Headline: the pile has 289 entries and zero edges. Nothing needs untangling; the question is whether to write the first one.

Soil now lifts an entry whose code area changes together with the areas the strongest matches are about. Coupling is computed from git log at draw time and stored nowhere, which is the point: every graph hugel has kept died with the store it lived in, and a weight derived on demand cannot be lost in a migration or go stale when the next commit lands. The thresholds are hugel_v2's, tuned against real repositories -- score 0.3, three shared commits, directory level, sweeping commits ignored.

It is a nudge and only a nudge: at full coupling an entry gains a sixth, enough to settle a near-tie and never enough to float something irrelevant. A draw with no coupling above threshold returns exactly what it returned before, which is tested in its own right.

Honest about what it does today: nothing. Only 41 of 289 entries record a path, and probing the live pile with six realistic queries changed no score and no order. The mechanism is right and the data is thin. The fix is upstream and filed.
